description: Learn how to read New York cannabis labels with BUZZY. Master THC/CBD potency, serving sizes, batch info, QR codes, and COAs. Read our guide.
h1: How to Read a New York Cannabis Label
excerpt: A legal cannabis package in New York contains a lot of information. Some of it is required for compliance, some helps you compare products, and some is there to make sure you know exactly how much cannabis is in a serving or package.
html:
A legal cannabis package in New York contains a lot of information. Some of it is required for compliance, some helps you compare products, and some is there to make sure you know exactly how much cannabis is in a serving or package.

Shop BUZZY’s Brooklyn cannabis menu →

Once you know what to look for, the label becomes one of the best tools for shopping more intentionally.

Start with the New York universal symbol

Regulated adult-use cannabis products sold through licensed New York dispensaries carry the state’s universal cannabis symbol. It is one of the quickest visual signs that a product belongs to the regulated New York market.

Find THC and CBD amounts

New York packaging includes cannabinoid information such as the amount of THC and CBD in the product. How that information is expressed depends on the format. Flower may show potency as a percentage, while an edible or beverage may show milligrams per serving and milligrams in the full package.

For anything portioned into servings, pay close attention to the difference between one serving and the entire container. A package containing multiple servings is not necessarily intended to be consumed all at once.

Look at serving size

For edibles and beverages, serving information is one of the most useful parts of the package. Check how many servings are in the container and how much THC is in each serving before consuming.

If you are new to a product, follow the label directions and give the product adequate time before considering more. Ingested cannabis can take longer to be felt than inhaled cannabis, and individual response varies.

Check the ingredients

Edibles, beverages, vapes, and other formulated products should include applicable ingredient information. This is especially important if you have food allergies or simply want to understand what else is in the product beyond cannabis.

Find the lot or batch information

Regulated products include identifying production information such as a processor’s lot number. Batch-level information supports traceability and connects the package to testing and production records.

Scan the QR code for the CoA

New York regulated cannabis products include a QR code or link to a Certificate of Analysis, or CoA. The CoA provides lab-testing information for the product or batch. OCM requires cannabis products to pass applicable laboratory testing before sale through licensed adult-use or medical dispensaries.

Depending on the report, you may see cannabinoid results and testing for contaminants or other required analytes. You do not need to become a lab scientist; the important habit is knowing that the testing record exists and is accessible.

Do not treat THC as a quality score

A higher THC number does not automatically mean better flower, a better vape, or a better experience. THC is one piece of the label. For flower in particular, aroma, terpene expression, freshness, cultivation, genetics, cure, and personal preference can all be more useful than choosing by potency alone.

What about indica, sativa, and hybrid?

Those labels can be useful as broad retail shorthand, but they are not a complete prediction of how a product will feel for every person. Use them as one data point alongside cannabinoids, terpenes, format, serving size, and your own past experience.

Ask if something does not make sense

Cannabis packaging is dense by design. If you cannot tell whether a number applies to a serving or the whole package, if you want help finding the CoA, or if two products look nearly identical on paper, ask your budtender to walk through them with you.

At BUZZY, we would rather help you understand a label than have you buy based on the biggest number on the front. Better information makes for a better-curated experience.

For educational purposes only; not medical advice. Product effects vary. Follow package directions and New York’s adult-use rules.
